**The Weight of a Single Word**

There’s a moment, just before dawn, when the world holds its breath. The air is thick with the kind of silence that isn’t absence but presence—an almost tangible thing, like the hum of a tuning fork just before the orchestra begins. I’ve always loved that moment. It’s the only time I feel like I’m not just *in* the world, but *part* of it, a single thread in some vast, unraveling tapestry.

Words have weight. Not the kind you measure on a scale, but the kind that settles in your chest, heavy as a stone dropped into still water. I’ve spent years collecting them—words, I mean—like a magpie hoarding shiny things. Some are sharp, like *lacerate* or *shatter*, words that feel like they could draw blood if you held them too tightly. Others are soft, like *murmur* or *dusk*, words that dissolve on the tongue like sugar. And then there are the ones that don’t fit neatly into either category, the ones that resist definition, like *longing* or *home*. Those are the dangerous ones. Those are the ones that can unravel you if you let them.

I used to think language was a tool, something we wielded to shape the world. But the older I get, the more I realize it’s the other way around. Words shape *us*. They carve grooves into our minds, dictate the way we see, the way we love, the way we hurt. A single word can be a lifeline or a noose. *Forgive.* *Never.* *Stay.* *Leave.* Say any of them aloud, and watch how the air around you shifts, like the first ripple in a pond.

There’s a story I heard once, about a man who lost his voice. Not in the way you’d think—not from illness or injury, but from choice. He woke up one morning and decided he was done with words. No more speaking, no more writing, no more signing. Just silence. At first, people thought it was a phase. Then they thought it was a protest. Then they stopped thinking about it at all. But the man didn’t care. He had realized something: that words were a kind of prison. They boxed things in, made them smaller than they were. A tree wasn’t just a *tree*—it was a *sycamore* or an *oak* or a *weeping willow*, each label narrowing its infinite possibility into something digestible, something *known*. The man wanted to live in the unknowable. So he stopped naming things.

I’ve thought about that man a lot. Mostly because I envy him.

Because I *love* words. I love the way they feel in my mouth, the way they can build entire worlds from nothing. I love the way a well-placed *but* can flip a sentence on its head, the way *maybe* can soften the blow of a *no*. But sometimes, I wonder if we’ve lost something in our obsession with naming. If, in our rush to define, we’ve forgotten how to simply *be*.

Take *love*, for example. What a ridiculous word. Four letters, one syllable, and yet it’s supposed to encompass everything from the way your heart stutters when you see someone across a crowded room to the quiet, bone-deep comfort of a decades-long marriage. It’s supposed to hold the ferocity of a mother’s protection and the gentle ache of missing someone who’s gone. How can one word possibly contain all that? And yet, we use it all the time. *I love coffee.* *I love that song.* *I love you.* We dilute it until it means nothing at all.

Or take *time*. We measure it in seconds and minutes and years, but what is it, really? A river? A thief? A healer? All of the above, and none. Time is the only thing we can’t control, and yet we act like we can—like we can *spend* it, *waste* it, *save* it, as if it’s currency instead of something far more precious and fleeting. We say *time flies*, but that’s not quite right. Time doesn’t fly. *We* do. We’re the ones hurtling forward, always looking back, always reaching for something just out of grasp.

I’ve been thinking a lot about memory lately. About how unreliable it is, how malleable. How a single word can reshape an entire past. *Always.* *Never.* *Forever.* Say them, and suddenly a moment becomes a monument, a fleeting feeling becomes an eternal truth. But memories aren’t facts. They’re stories we tell ourselves, edited and re-edited until they fit the narrative we need. And words are the tools we use to do the editing.

There’s a line from a poem I read once—*We die. That may be the meaning of life. But we do language. That may be the measure of our lives.* I’ve carried that with me for years. It haunts me, in the best way. Because what does it mean, to *do* language? Is it enough to speak, to write, to string words together like beads on a necklace? Or is there something more? Something deeper, something that requires us to listen—not just to others, but to the silence between the words, to the things left unsaid?

I don’t know. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the beauty of words is that they can’t contain everything. Maybe their power lies in what they *can’t* say.

There’s a game I used to play as a child. I’d close my eyes and point to a random word in the dictionary, then try to write a story around it. Once, I landed on *abyss*. I was eight years old, and I had no idea what it meant. But the word itself was so heavy, so *dark*, that I knew it was important. So I wrote a story about a girl who fell into an abyss and discovered that it wasn’t a place of nothingness, but a place of *everything*—all the things people had lost or forgotten or thrown away. It was the first time I understood that words could be doorways.

Now, I wonder if that’s what we’re all doing, in some way. Falling into abysses, building doorways, trying to make sense of the chaos. Maybe that’s what language is for—not to explain the world, but to give us a way to live inside it, even when it doesn’t make sense.

I don’t have any grand conclusions. No neat little bow to tie this up. Just this: words are magic. And like all magic, they can heal or they can destroy. They can build bridges or burn them down. They can make us feel less alone, or they can isolate us in our own heads. The trick, I think, is to use them wisely. To remember that for every word we say, there’s a word we don’t. For every story we tell, there’s one we leave untold.

And maybe, just maybe, that’s where the real power lies. Not in the words themselves, but in the spaces between them. In the silence. In the unspoken.

In the weight of what we choose not to say.
